profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the application delivery stream and the platform engineering stream at a company building a multi-cloud risk-management service used by enterprise teams to log delivery risks and mitigation actions. The next milestone is an internal pilot for an airline scheduling customer, and the workflow service needs to be handed from the app team to the platform team for deployment through the shared release path spanning AWS and Azure. Context: the feature design and cloud architecture were already settled in earlier planning; this meeting is only to line up the handoff details, expected artifacts, environment target, and ownership for rollout-related risk tracking. Agenda: confirm which integration environment the next drop is meant for, what Helm release artifacts will be handed over on Thursday, note any assumptions around integration test status before platform intake, and make sure the shared risk register stays current for cloud-specific rollout issues. Expected outcome: both participants leave believing they have aligned on the handoff package, target environment, test status, and risk-register ownership for next week's integration push.

members.name: Nina Alvarez
members.expertise: Backend workflow services, release coordination, Kubernetes-based application delivery
members.background: Nina leads the team implementing the risk-mitigation workflow engine and related APIs; before joining the company, she worked at a SaaS firm where product teams handed off application charts to a central platform group after validating behavior in a team-owned integration cluster.
members.private_state: She wants to keep the pilot feature on schedule without pulling engineers into extra packaging or environment work, and she is trying to avoid any surprise scope increase because two senior developers are already covering an unrelated production issue.
hidden_assumptions: The 'integration environment' means her team's long-lived shared app integration cluster, which is close enough to production for feature validation but does not include the full cross-cloud platform controls.

The 'Helm release artifacts' are the reusable chart, image tag, and standard release notes emitted by the application CI pipeline; cloud bindings and environment overlays are downstream platform concerns.
If someone asks whether integration tests have passed, the relevant signal is the app team's contract and workflow tests running against mocked cloud dependencies and the team integration cluster.
The shared risk register is maintained in a federated way, so each team logs risks originating in its own workstream and platform-specific rollout risks are normally added by platform.

members.name: Victor Chen
members.expertise: Multi-cloud deployment platforms, release governance, compliance automation
members.background: Victor manages the internal platform that provisions and deploys services across AWS and Azure; he previously worked in a regulated fintech environment where application teams supplied environment-ready release bundles and platform intake assumed testing had already exercised the real shared integration stack.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid late surprises in the pilot environment and make sure the application team uses the standard multi-cloud release path cleanly, because security and operations are scrutinizing this pilot as a model for future cross-cloud services.
hidden_assumptions: The 'integration environment' refers to the shared cross-cloud integration stage managed by platform, where AWS and Azure wiring, policy checks, and traffic components are enabled together.
The 'Helm release artifacts' include not only the base chart and image tag but also the target-environment values, secret references for both clouds, and rollback metadata needed for platform intake.

If integration tests are said to have passed, that means the service has already been exercised in the real shared integration environment with actual cloud bindings rather than mocked dependencies alone.
The feature delivery lead is the default owner of the shared risk-register entry end-to-end, including platform-related rollout risks once they may affect the feature timeline.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss getting the next drop into 'the integration environment' next week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the application team's own shared integration cluster used for realistic workflow validation before platform promotion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the platform-managed cross-cloud integration environment spanning AWS and Azure with shared routing, policy enforcement, and cloud wiring enabled.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both teams routinely use the phrase 'integration environment' as if it were singular and obvious; in a coordination meeting focused on timing and handoff, the term sounds settled enough that neither person feels a need to define it.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the Helm release artifacts
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree Nina will send over 'the Helm release artifacts' by Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes the base Helm chart, versioned image tag, and ordinary release notes produced by the app pipeline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes those items plus environment-specific values files, cloud secret bindings, and rollback metadata required to admit the release into the platform workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds precise and tool-specific, which creates false confidence that there is already a shared convention; each person assumes the other is operating from the same internal template.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to the feature being fine once 'integration tests have passed' before intake.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 takes this to mean the application workflow and API integration suite passed against mocked cloud dependencies and the team integration cluster.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 takes this to mean the service has already been exercised against the actual shared multi-cloud integration setup with real cloud-side bindings in place.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither disagrees that integration testing matters, and both consider their own test scope the normal meaning of the phrase; because the meeting is about coordination rather than test planning, the exact boundary of 'integration' remains implicit.

misalignment_points.topic: Default owner for updating the shared risk register
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss 'updating the risk register' for rollout concerns.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes each team updates the register for risks it directly owns, so platform-side rollout concerns will be logged by Victor's team when needed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the feature delivery lead owns the single register entry and should record even platform-originated risks once they may influence the pilot schedule or rollout confidence.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They already agree the risk register exists and should stay current, so the latent disagreement is only about the default RACI boundary, which usually follows team custom and therefore goes unstated.
